name: New York Academy of Art
watch: Epstein sat on the board from 1987 to 1994. After his 2008 conviction he paid $65,900 for events in 2012 and 2014, the Academy says.
why_flagged: Van Cleef & Arpels sponsors its Tribeca Ball for scholarships. Epstein, a board member 1987 to 1994, paid $65,900 for events in 2012 and 2014, the Academy says.
records_note: Form 990s and a 2025 audit are on ProPublica.
finances_note: FY2025 income USD 8.8M: about 72 percent earned (tuition), 30 percent donations, under 1 percent government grants; events and other items net negative (Form 990, Part VIII).

overview: Graduate school of figurative and representational art at 111 Franklin Street in Tribeca, New York (school website).
Instruction began in 1980 as the New York Drawing Association. Stuart Pivar is credited as primary founder and Andy Warhol as a key founder and funder (Wikipedia).
Building: a five-storey, 42,000 square foot building designed by Benjamin Warner in 1861. The school began operating there in 1990, and a 2001 fire damaged half the interior (Wikipedia).
Programmes: a two-year MFA with about 100 students, a one-year Certificate of Fine Art, a four-week summer programme and continuing education classes (school website; Wikipedia).
Public events: the Tribeca Ball, first held in 1994, and the Take Home a Nude auction at Sotheby's (Wikipedia). Chubb Fellows exhibitions are listed on the school site.
The school's site lists studio tours booked online.
details.funding_verdict: New York Academy of Art: privately funded: tuition, fundraising events, foundations and individual donors
funding: Warhol's bequest after his death in 1987 let the school buy its Franklin Street headquarters, and the Warhol Foundation had given more than $1 million by 2004. Pivar gave key early support (Wikipedia).
Van Cleef & Arpels was title sponsor of the 15 April 2025 Tribeca Ball (Tribeca Citizen, 11 April 2025, a post labelled as sponsored by the Academy). The post does not call the ball a fundraiser.

red_flags.heading: Jeffrey Epstein
points: Epstein sat on the Academy's board from 1987 to 1994 (Hyperallergic, Rhea Nayyar, 16 March 2026).

After his 2008 Florida guilty plea, Epstein paid $25,000 for a Tribeca Ball table in each of 2012 and 2014 and $30,000 to the Portrait Scholarship fund in 2014, after an invitation from Eileen Guggenheim (Hyperallergic, Rhea Nayyar, 16 March 2026). These examples come to $80,000 and do not reconcile with the $65,900 total, which Hyperallergic describes as Epstein's contributions to events in 2012 and 2014; the article does not explain the difference. It adds that the Academy gave $30,000 to the charity in 2020 to match the 2014 scholarship gift.

In March 2026 the Academy redirected $65,900 to Girls Educational and Mentoring Services (GEMS), a nonprofit supporting sexually exploited and trafficked girls and young women; its statement to alumni was dated 12 March. Board members agreed to match the sum so student resources were not cut (USA Art News, 16 March 2026).

The board's email cited "serious failures in judgment and governance" and said the Academy should not have accepted the contributions; the Academy said it would develop an ethics committee to review donor-support policies (Hyperallergic).
Board chair Eileen Guggenheim stepped down on 1 April 2026, a month earlier than planned, and remains on the board (USA Art News).

Unverified: alumna Maria Farmer alleges Guggenheim introduced her to Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell in 1995 and told her to sell Epstein a painting at a discount; USA Art News reports Guggenheim denies introducing them and does not recall the conversation. Hyperallergic says Farmer filed a report with the FBI that went ignored for a decade.

A petition to remove Guggenheim as chair collected more than 2,100 signatures; the Academy called it "filled with false information, innuendo, and lies". Its organiser retracted it (Hyperallergic, Hakim Bishara, 7 May 2020, with a note dated 17 February 2021).

press.overall: The criticism in art media is about Epstein and the Academy's governance; no critique of the school's teaching or funders other than Epstein was found.

items.title: Hakim Bishara, "Petition Calls for Removal of New York Academy of Art Board Chair, Citing Jeffrey Epstein Ties" (2020)
points: Reports the petition by Kirby Sommers backing Maria Farmer and asking for Guggenheim's removal, plus the Academy's rebuttal.
Notes the petition was later retracted.

items.title: Rhea Nayyar, "New York Academy of Art Says It Will Donate Epstein Money" (2026)
points: Reports the redirection of $65,900, the board's admission of failures, and Guggenheim's early exit.
Sets out Farmer's account; it includes no denial from Guggenheim.

details.bottom_line: The school's regular money is private and little of it is published. The documented problem is Epstein: he sat on the board from 1987 to 1994 and paid for Academy events after his 2008 plea, which the Academy's board now calls a failure of judgment; it redirected $65,900 to a charity in March 2026. Watch the new ethics committee and whether the Academy publishes a donor list.

name: Noguchi Museum
funding: The museum was awarded $4.5 million in capital funding in 2022, $1.5 million of it from Mayor Eric Adams.
watch: In September 2024 the museum fired three gallery attendants for wearing keffiyehs. Jhumpa Lahiri then declined its 2024 Isamu Noguchi Award.
records_note: Names its trustees and posts dated benefit donor listings; only ProPublica filings for 2003 to 2025 were opened.
finances_note: Calendar 2024 income USD 19.4M: about 5 percent government grants, 4 percent other donations, 36 percent earned (net sales of inventory plus admissions), 51 percent investment return (Form 990).
highlight: Isamu Noguchi designed and created this museum and sculpture garden at 32-37 Vernon Boulevard in Long Island City.

overview: Museum and sculpture garden of the work of Isamu Noguchi at 32-37 Vernon Boulevard, Long Island City, Queens (Wikipedia).

Chartered as The Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum. It opened to the public in 1985, initially on a seasonal basis, and was the first museum of its kind established in America by a living artist (Wikipedia).
Named for its founder, the sculptor Isamu Noguchi, who bought a former photogravure plant and gas station across the street from his studio in 1974 (Wikipedia).
Building: a two-storey building of about 24,000 square feet with a sculpture garden. A $13.5 million capital master plan was approved in 1999, and the museum reopened in June 2004 (Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: Noguchi Museum: mainly self-generated: its own assets, merchandise sales and some city capital grants
funding: Form 990 for 2024: revenue $19,394,466, of which contributions were $1,822,009, sales of assets $7,985,372 and net inventory sales $6,191,425; expenses $11,800,874; net assets $79,074,060 (ProPublica).

In 2022 the museum received $4.5 million in capital funding to restore Noguchi's 1959 studio and build a collection and archive building: about $1.5 million from Mayor Eric Adams and the rest from Queens Borough President Donovan Richards (Wikipedia).

red_flags.heading: 2024 keffiyeh ban, firings and boycott
points: ArtReview reported the museum introduced a dress code on 14 August 2024 barring political messages on staff clothing and emailed its 72 employees; The Art Newspaper said the policy was updated in August.

A petition against it was signed by about two thirds of the 72-person staff (The Art Newspaper, Anni Irish, 11 September 2024) or by 54 staff (ArtReview). On 21 August, 14 staff walked off the job according to The Art Newspaper; ArtReview counted eight.

Three gallery attendants were fired on 4 September 2024 after refusing to follow the dress code; Hyperallergic says they were fired for wearing keffiyehs (Valentina Di Liscia, 26 September 2024). A museum spokesperson told The Art Newspaper, "Given this pertains to personnel matters, we are unable to provide further details" (The Art Newspaper).
On 8 September supporters rallied outside the museum, calling for director Amy Hau to step down (The Art Newspaper).

Author Jhumpa Lahiri declined the 2024 Isamu Noguchi Award in support of the fired workers; a spokesperson said: "We respect her perspective and understand that this policy may or may not align with everyone's views" (Hyperallergic, 26 September 2024).

Staff petitioned for a union vote with UAW Local 2110 (Hyperallergic, Isa Farfan, 16 December 2024) and won a unanimous National Labor Relations Board election, announced on 13 January 2025. The museum said it "acknowledges and respects our staff's decision to unionize" (Hyperallergic, Isa Farfan, 15 January 2025).

press.overall: Art media coverage reports the ban, the firings and the protests; none of it concerns the museum's funders.

items.title: Anni Irish (2024), report on the Noguchi Museum's dress code and firings
points: Reports the policy, the walkout, the three dismissals, and that a fourth employee, the director of visitor services, was also terminated, without saying whether that was linked.
News report; the museum gave a statement on personnel matters only.

items.title: Valentina Di Liscia, "Author Jhumpa Lahiri Turns Down Noguchi Award Over Keffiyeh Ban" (2024)
points: Reports Lahiri's refusal and fired attendant Trasonia Abbott's hope that Lee Ufan would also reject the award.

items.title: Isa Farfan, "Noguchi Museum Workers Move to Unionize" (2024)
points: Staff cite a need for "greater transparency" and "better conditions"; the museum had not replied to a request for comment.

items.title: "Noguchi Museum fires three for wearing keffiyehs" (2024)
points: Reports the petition signed by 54 staff, the walkout of eight (a figure that differs from The Art Newspaper's 14) and a Sunday protest outside the museum calling for director Amy Hau to step down.
No museum statement in the piece.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the museum looks clean: it rests on its own assets, merchandise sales and city capital grants, with no sponsor of concern found. The weak point is governance of staff: the 2024 political dress ban, the three firings and the boycott by Jhumpa Lahiri. Watch whether the museum publishes a donor list and how its dealings with the new union develop.

name: Queens Museum
funding: The City of New York owns the building. The New York City Department of Cultural Affairs and the New York State Council on the Arts fund it in part.
watch: In 2017 the museum cancelled, then reinstated, an Israeli UN Mission event. In 2023, 17 staff signed a letter and several joined a strike.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
records_note: Names its public funders with no date and lists its trustees; no annual report on the site, Form 990s for 2001 to 2025 on ProPublica.
finances_note: FY2024-25 income USD 7.79M: about 67 percent government grants, 29 percent other donations and gifts, 3 percent earned (Form 990, Part VIII).
highlight: A building from the 1939 New York World's Fair houses the 9,335-square-foot Panorama of the City of New York.

overview: Art museum and educational centre in the New York City Building in Flushing Meadows Corona Park, Queens, on the site of the 1939-40 and 1964-65 World's Fairs. The building is owned by the City of New York (museum website).
Opened in November 1972 as the Queens County Art and Cultural Center and was renamed the Queens Museum in 1973 (Wikipedia).

The building was designed by Aymar Embury II as the New York City Pavilion for the 1939 World's Fair. It housed the UN General Assembly from 1946 to 1951 (Wikipedia). The 1947 UN vote on the partition of Palestine took place on the site (Hyperallergic).
Open Wednesday to Friday 12 pm to 5 pm and Saturday and Sunday 11 am to 5 pm. Closed Monday and Tuesday (museum website). Wikipedia states that admission is pay what you want.
details.funding_verdict: Queens Museum: public funds from New York City, New York State and Queens officials, plus members and trustees
funding: The museum website states that its support comes in part from the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs, with assistance from the Queens Borough President and the New York City Council, and from the New York State Council on the Arts. It also lists the Board of Trustees, members and friends.

Capital money: Wikipedia lists $10.6 million from Queens Borough President Helen Marshall in 2006, $26.4 million from the city in 2021, and $8.5 million each from the city (2023) and the state (2025) for the Suna Children's Museum wing. Hyperallergic confirms the $26.4 million city award of 2021 for the second phase of expansion.

red_flags.heading: Protest or boycott
points: 2017: the museum cancelled, then reinstated, an on-site event organised by Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, to commemorate the 70th anniversary of Israel's founding with a reenactment of the 1947 UN partition vote. Hyperallergic, citing the Jerusalem Post, reported that director Laura Raicovich told Danon she was reversing her approval, citing concerns from "Palestinian friends of the museum", and that her message said the board had voted not to hold a "political event." Danon called for her immediate dismissal. Councilman Rory Lancman and Assemblyman Michael Simanowitz called the decision "a disgrace and a violation of law." After what the museum described as a "productive conversation" with Danon, it reversed its decision and said it would work with the Israeli Mission on the commemoration (Hyperallergic, Claire Voon, 18 August 2017).

2023: in October, 17 Queens Museum employees signed a letter asking leadership to address the building's history as the site of the 1947 UN vote and to speak publicly on Palestine. Several signatories joined a strike for Palestine on 20 October. Staff then described heightened surveillance, and the director said circulating the letter and strike call by museum email broke museum policy. At a staff meeting on 16 November Tallant said the museum "is not able to make political statements" and cited its nonprofit status, its bylaws and the American Alliance of Museums code of ethics (Hyperallergic, Maya Pontone, 17 November 2023).

press.overall: Hyperallergic reported two episodes in which the museum was criticised: by Israeli and New York officials in 2017, and by its own staff in 2023.

items.title: Claire Voon, "Queens Museum Cancels, Then Reinstates Israel-Sponsored Event After Accusations of Antisemitism" (2017)
points: Reports that the museum cancelled an on-site event for the 70th anniversary of Israel's founding, organised by Danon, and reversed the decision after objections from Danon and New York officials, including Comptroller Scott Stringer, who said it sent "a disappointing message."
Reports the museum's statement that it would work with the Israeli Mission on the commemoration of the 1947 vote.

items.title: Maya Pontone, "Queens Museum Director Declines to Issue Statement on Gaza" (2023)
points: Reports a staff letter signed by 17 employees, a strike on 20 October 2023 and staff accounts of surveillance.
The museum declined to issue a statement on Palestine.

details.bottom_line: The documented money behind the Queens Museum is a city-owned building, public funds from the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs, the Queens Borough President, the City Council and the New York State Council on the Arts, capital grants from the city and state, plus members and trustees. The documented points are the two protest episodes, the 2017 pressure over the cancelled Israeli Mission event and the 2023 staff letter and strike over the museum's silence on Palestine.

name: Utah Museum of Fine Arts
funding: A unit of the University of Utah and the state's fine arts museum. The pages read did not state its budget or funders; a Mellon Foundation grant supported the joint Museum+Library Search with the Marriott Library (museum website).
watch: A University of Utah museum that moved into the 74,000-square-foot Price building in 2001, with more than 22,000 original works.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Utah Museum of Fine Arts, in the Marcia and John Price Museum Building, 410 Campus Center Drive, on the University of Utah campus; 74,000 square feet, occupied since 2001 (museum website).
A small gallery opened in 1914 in the university's Park Building; it was incorporated as the Utah Museum of Fine Arts and reopened in 1951 (museum website).

What is there: more than 22,000 original works; a gift of art from Winifred Kimball Hudnut is named; rights and reproduction requests for Spiral Jetty and Sun Tunnels go to the Dia Art Foundation (museum website).

Archive: Museum+Library Search covers the museum and the Marriott Library catalogs, from a joint initiative supported by a Mellon Foundation grant; the museum publishes a list of deaccessioned artworks; collections visits are paused until March 2027 because of construction (museum website).
details.funding_verdict: Utah Museum of Fine Arts: University of Utah and the state, with a Mellon Foundation grant for its catalog
funding: It is the fine arts museum for both the State of Utah and the University of Utah (museum website).
No reporting found in the pages read of the museum's budget, donors or a Form 990.
details.bottom_line: A university museum; the pages read give no budget or donors beyond a Mellon Foundation grant. No controversy was found in the sources read.

name: Kuindzhi Art Museum
funding: A Ukrainian city museum until 2022. Under Russian occupation it is run by the culture ministry of the so-called Donetsk People's Republic, which the US, EU and UK sanction.
watch: Its Kuindzhi paintings were taken to a museum in Donetsk after the city fell in 2022.
why_flagged: A Ukrainian city museum until 2022. Under Russian occupation it is run by the culture ministry of the so-called Donetsk People's Republic, which the US, EU and UK sanction.
records_note: The museum was destroyed in March 2022 and no official site, report, accounts, funder list or board turned up.

overview: Museum dedicated to the painter Arkhip Kuindzhi, born in Mariupol. Bellingcat places it a few blocks from the Drama Theatre, destroyed in an airstrike on 16 March 2022.
Opened on 30 October 2010 as a branch of the Mariupol Museum of Local Lore. The idea was first proposed in 1914, the premises were donated in 1997 and renovation began in 2008 (Wikipedia).
Collection: about 650 paintings, 960 graphic works, 150 sculptures and over 300 decorative objects, with works by Aivazovsky, Vereshchagin and Shishkin (Wikipedia).

Damage: on 23 March 2022 Mariupol's city council said a Russian bomb had destroyed the museum. Bellingcat's satellite imagery of 24 April shows the building damaged, not razed, and Bellingcat could not identify the weapon or establish who was responsible. Wikipedia says the exhibition had been moved to the basement and lists the museum as dissolved in 2022.
details.funding_verdict: Kuindzhi Art Museum: state-run: a municipal branch museum until 2022, then, according to a sign at its door, under the culture ministry of the Donetsk People's Republic
funding: Until 2022 it was a branch of the city's Museum of Local Lore (Wikipedia).
Under occupation, Bellingcat reports only the sign naming the DNR "Ministry of Culture"; no reporting found of a budget, accounts or board.

red_flags.heading: Sanctions on the occupying body, DNR
points: The Donetsk People's Republic (DNR) was added to the US Treasury's SDN list on 16 July 2014 (OFAC). It is also listed by the EU under Council Regulation 269/2014 and by the UK, both from 25 July 2014 (Black Sea News sanctions database).
The only source for the DNR running the museum is the handwritten sign at the door that Bellingcat saw in 2022, which placed it under the DNR "Ministry of Culture".

red_flags.heading: Removal of the paintings to Donetsk
points: Lina Garmash of the Donetsk History Museum said 25 paintings from Mariupol, including three Kuindzhis, are in storage there (The Moscow Times).
Alexander Mozgovoi, a DNR television anchor, said the works were taken to Donetsk for safekeeping and "Nothing has been stolen" (The Moscow Times).

On 27 April 2022 Petro Andriushchenko, an adviser to Mariupol's mayor, said on Telegram that Natalia Kapustnikova, director of the Museum of Local Lore, had handed the paintings to the occupiers; she told Izvestiya the paintings were safe (Bellingcat). In June 2023 the EU Council sanctioned her, saying she "gave those works willingly over to the Russian authorities" without the consent of Ukrainian authorities or the Kuindzhi museum's director (Justice Info).

press.overall: The coverage reports its destruction and the removal of its paintings.

items.title: Elaine Velie, "Ukraine Accuses Russia of Looting Over 2,000 Artworks" (2022)
points: Reports the Mariupol City Council's claim, from its Telegram post, that Russian forces took over 2,000 works from three museums to Donetsk.
Reports no Russian response. Unverified: that the director of the Mariupol Museum of Local History handed over the three Kuindzhi paintings, from a city official who is not named in the piece.

items.title: Yanina Sorokina, "How Russia 'Removed' Priceless Kuindzhi Artworks from Ukraine's Mariupol" (2022)
points: Reports pro-Kremlin media footage of DNR culture minister Zheltyakov, the anchor Mozgovoi and men in balaclavas packing paintings in Mariupol, and gives the Donetsk museum's own account of storing them.
Not art criticism: a news investigation.

wider_context: Justice Info (Shahida Tulaganova, 2025) reports that over 2,000 artefacts were removed from the Kuindzhi museum to temporary storage in Donetsk, and that the EU sanctioned four museum directors in June 2023 over transfers of Ukrainian collections.
The Kuindzhi museum is the museum whose works the EU Council's 2023 statement on Kapustnikova names, which connects it to these sanctions.
details.bottom_line: There is no private funder to assess: the museum was a city branch until 2022 and now stands, damaged, under a body the US, EU and UK sanction, on the evidence of one handwritten sign. The weak points are the removal of its Kuindzhi paintings to Donetsk and the lack of any published budget or governance. Worth watching: whether the paintings return to Ukraine.

name: PinchukArtCentre
funding: Private centre founded in 2006 and run by the Victor Pinchuk Foundation. Pinchuk's fortune comes from Interpipe, a maker of steel pipes and railway wheels.
watch: Father-in-law Leonid Kuchma authorised the 2004 Kryvorizhstal sale to Pinchuk and Akhmetov; rivals called it below market. 2020: two prize nominees quit over dismissed guides.
why_flagged: Father-in-law Leonid Kuchma authorised the 2004 Kryvorizhstal sale to Pinchuk and Akhmetov; rivals called it below market. 2020: two prize nominees quit over dismissed guides.
records_note: No records of its own: its founder's Victor Pinchuk Foundation posts annual reports from 2009 to 2018; the centre lists staff, no funders or board.

overview: Private contemporary art centre in the Besarabka area of Kyiv, at Velyka Vasylkivska 1/3-2 (Wikipedia).
Founded by Victor Pinchuk, who consolidated his philanthropy under the Victor Pinchuk Foundation in 2006. The centre opened on 16 September 2006 (Wikipedia).
Occupies a historic complex with interiors by Philippe Chiambaretta, on six floors with more than 3,000 sq m of exhibition space (the centre site).
On site: exhibition halls, a library, an education room and a video lounge. Programmes include the Research Platform (since 2016) and two prizes.
Closed for 143 days after Russia's full-scale invasion of 24 February 2022 and reopened on 17 July 2022 (Wikipedia).
Visiting: free admission. Wednesday to Sunday, 12 pm to 9 pm, last entry 8:30 pm. Closed during air alerts.
details.funding_verdict: PinchukArtCentre: self-funded: founder Victor Pinchuk, through his foundation
funding: The centre site names Pinchuk as founder.
Pinchuk's fortune: he founded Interpipe, a producer of seamless pipes and railway wheels, and with his wife is the largest shareholder of StarLightMedia (Wikipedia).

red_flags.heading: Protest after dismissal of guides
points: October 2019: guides, whom Wikipedia calls mediators, formed a union. 25 December 2019: union members protested near the centre and gave management a letter asking for talks on a collective agreement. Their fixed-term contracts were not renewed and on 9 February 2020 management announced it was cancelling the position (Wikipedia). The Art Newspaper (28 February 2020) reported 28 guides dismissed; the Kyiv Post (23 February 2020) said about 20.
The centre denies the allegations and says an internal review in September 2019 led to the decision (The Art Newspaper).
Two nominees for the 2020 PinchukArtCentre Prize, Valentina Petrova and Pavlo Grazhdanskij, withdrew in solidarity (The Art Newspaper; Kyiv Post).

red_flags.heading: Founder's ties to the Kuchma privatisations and US donations
points: In 2004 the state sold the Kryvorizhstal steel plant to Pinchuk and Rinat Akhmetov for $800 million (Kyiv Post). Kuchma was president at the time and Pinchuk is married to his daughter Olena Pinchuk (Wikipedia; its Pinchuk page carries a neutrality banner).

The state took the plant back in June 2005 after President Yushchenko called the 2004 sale a theft, and Mittal Steel bought it at a televised auction on 24 October 2005 for more than $4.8 billion (AP via NBC News).

Trump Foundation: tax returns released on 22 November 2016 showed a $150,000 gift from the Victor Pinchuk Foundation, which its chairman Thomas Weihe said supported Trump's video appearance at the Yalta European Strategy meeting in Kyiv on 11 September 2015 (Kyiv Post).

Unverified: Ihor Kolomoisky said at a parliamentary hearing in March 2015 that Pinchuk received a bribe of $5 million a month for the rights to manage Ukrnafta; the National Anti-Corruption Bureau opened proceedings on 18 March 2015 (Wikipedia). syg.ma states that Pinchuk has never been charged.

press.overall: Little criticism in the established art press; the substantive critiques are a 2020 report on the guides dispute and a 2026 opinion essay on a community platform.

items.title: Dorian Batycka, "PinchukArtCenter employees claim to have been sacked after attempting to form trade union" (2020)
points: 28 guides were dismissed after forming a union at the end of October 2019; union head Anastasia Bondarenko alleges threats, denied sick leave and precarious contracts.
The centre denies the allegations; two prize nominees withdrew.

items.title: Toma Istomina, "Pinchuk Art Center mediators lose jobs after forming union" (2020)
points: Petrova called the centre "a PR project of oligarch Pinchuk" and questioned how a jury could assess twenty works in a day; Grazhdanskij said its avoidance of public discussion raised questions about the prize's transparency.

items.title: artur.sumarokov, "The Pinchuk Art Centre: Two Decades of Cynical Art-Washing for Ukraine's Most Polished Oligarch" (2026)
points: Argues the centre launders reputation earned from Kuchma-era privatisations, and that Western institutions that took Pinchuk's money enabled it.
Openly adversarial opinion essay by an individual author, not reporting; several claims are not documented.

details.bottom_line: No reporting found of an outside funder: Pinchuk's own money pays for the centre, and no budget or board is published. The weak points are the 2020 guides dismissal and prize withdrawals, and the founder's Kuchma-era privatisation and political donations. Worth watching: whether the centre publishes accounts or a board list.

name: Espacio de Arte Contemporáneo (EAC)
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: National public contemporary art space at Arenal Grande 1930, Montevideo, in the former Cárcel de Miguelete prison in the La Comercial neighbourhood (Wikipedia).

Opened on 27 July 2010. The project began in 2008 on an initiative driven by the National Directorate of Culture of the Ministry of Education and Culture (Wikipedia). Wikipedia calls it the only national public institution devoted exclusively to contemporary art.

The prison was designed by Juan Alberto Capurro and built in 1888 on Jeremy Bentham's panopticon model, with a central watchtower and four radial three-storey pavilions. It held inmates for over a century (Wikipedia). It is a national historic monument (Artefacto, 2021).

The EAC occupies the wing facing Arenal Grande. Wikipedia says a 2018 addition, Sala Seis, gives 160 square metres of exhibition space. Artefacto (substack account _artefacto, 19 August 2021) says the Natural History Museum joined the site in 2018.

Programmes: open calls for individual, collective and curatorial proposals, residencies, training and research, a public programme of talks, workshops and guided tours, and the LAB EAC. Since 2018 it has hosted the Premio Nacional de Artes Visuales exhibition (Wikipedia). The grounds include an open-air photo gallery from the CdF (Artefacto).

Galleries open Wednesday to Saturday 13:00 to 19:00. Plazas and photo gallery daily 9:00 to 19:00. Admission free (Ministry of Education and Culture notice, 23 March 2026). A ministry notice of 21 December 2023 for January and February gave Wednesday to Saturday 13:00 to 19:00 and Sunday 11:00 to 17:00.
details.funding_verdict: Espacio de Arte Contemporáneo: public: Uruguay's Ministry of Education and Culture
funding: The ministry owns the site and its National Directorate of Culture administers the EAC (Wikipedia).
Wikipedia states that the project received support from the Spanish Agency for International Development Cooperation (AECID).
details.bottom_line: The EAC is a state-run space of Uruguay's Ministry of Education and Culture, housed in a former prison.

name: The Factory Contemporary Arts Centre
funding: Founded 2016; self-funded social enterprise where art sales and an on-site cafe pay for programmes.
records_note: The live site returns an empty page; archived copies show no reports, accounts, donor list or board, only a founder and former curatorial staff.
affiliations_note: Co-organises the Pollination programme for young Southeast Asian curators and artists with ILHAM Gallery in Kuala Lumpur and MAIIAM in Chiang Mai.

overview: Independent contemporary art centre at 15 Nguyen U Di, Thao Dien ward, District 2, Ho Chi Minh City (e-flux directory; Viet Nam News).

Founded in 2016 by the artist Ti-A (Viet Nam News; Artribune). Zoe Butt is named artistic director in Art & Market (2018) and Artribune (2019). Artribune adds that she was previously executive director and curator at Sàn Art from 2009 to 2016.
It describes itself as the first purpose-built independent space for contemporary art in Vietnam (e-flux directory).

Building: HTAP Architects, with Hoanh Tran and Archie Pizzini as architects in charge, designed the 880 m² centre, completed in 2017 (ArchDaily). Viet Nam News describes a street front of coloured containers.

On site: exhibition spaces, an arts library, workshops, a co-working space, a restaurant and a bar (Viet Nam News, September 2017). Art & Market names The Glass Box, a private exhibition programme for collectors, a Reading Room, and the Pollination residency programme.
Visiting: the e-flux directory lists Tuesday to Sunday 10am to 7pm. Viet Nam News in 2017 gave entry as VND10,000 to VND100,000 depending on the activity.
details.funding_verdict: The Factory Contemporary Arts Centre: self-funded: a social enterprise paying for programmes from art sales and on-site businesses
funding: The centre says all profit from the sale of art and from the businesses on the property supports the running costs of its art programmes (Art & Market, 2018; Viet Nam News, 2017).
Artribune (2019) says the centre is not a commercial gallery, though it has sold works.

press.overall: Coverage is descriptive and positive, and the one piece that criticises anything criticises the setting in Vietnam, not the centre.

items.title: Redazione (editorial staff), "Ho Chi Minh City. The Factory Contemporary Arts Centre" (27 March 2019)
points: A first-person account by curatorial assistant Le Thien Bao (Lê Thiên Bảo). The criticism is of Vietnam's system: official education centres on socialist realism, the Minister of Culture gives consent to exhibit works judged of artistic value, every exhibition needs a licence to exhibit, and a work judged unsuitable cannot be shown but can go in a catalogue (translated from the Italian).
Criticises the context, not the institution. It reports no exhibition of the centre being refused or closed.

items.title: Ian Tee, "Social Enterprise Meets Art Infrastructure at The Factory" (2018)
points: Describes the social-enterprise model and the programmes. Names the limited arts infrastructure and financial support for artistic production in Vietnam as wider challenges.
Not criticism of the centre.

wider_context: Artribune (2019), in the words of the centre's curatorial assistant: in Vietnam every exhibition needs a licence to exhibit, the Minister of Culture gives consent, and a work judged unsuitable cannot be shown. This describes the licensing system for all exhibitions in Vietnam, not an act against the centre.
The centre works inside that system.
details.bottom_line: The centre's stated money is the founder's enterprise: art sales and an on-site restaurant and bar, with no named donor, state body or corporate sponsor. The weak points are that no accounts, board or funder list are published and the website returned no content on the date checked. Worth watching: whether the centre publishes a funder list and whether it still operates.
